newsitem.title: USA: American's jet issue seen having wide impact.
newsitem.headline: American's jet issue seen having wide impact.

text.p: The board of American Airlines' pilots will meet Friday to evaluate a proposed labor pact that offers a victory for the nation's second largest airline and could have broad implications for future airline labor negotiations, labor experts said.
The proposed settlement offers the pilots a moderate pay raise in exchange for a major concession on which pilots will fly the American Airlines' new regional jets, industry sources said.

Pending approval from the union's board and rank-and-file members, American has won the right to have its lower-paid American Eagle pilots fly the commuter jets, but on a restricted basis, industry sources said.

"This sets a standard for the industry. Small-haul units need a non-union or lower-cost environment," said Forrest Harding, a professor at California State University who specializes in airline issues.
American's expected regional jet victory could give other airlines, such as US Airways Group Inc, greater leverage in negotiating proposals to set up low-cost units.
US Airways is in talks with its pilots union concerning wage concessions and plans to set up a low-cost unit.
US Airways could American's expected labor pact as further ammunition in its fight to cut costs and gain productivity concessions from its pilots, industry analysts said.
The issue of which pilots will fly American Airline's new commuter jets has been a contentious issue during negotiations and has been closely watched by the industry.
"The money is not at the heart of this," Harding said. "The regional jet issue has been the issue that has been, at times, a very personal issue in the talks."
American, a unit of AMR Corp, insisted it needed lower-paid pilots from its American Eagle unit to fly the commuter jets to compete with other low-cost carriers.
But the Allied Pilots Association feared that, if American succeeded in its demands, many of routes flown by the mainline pilots eventually would be lost to the American Eagle unit.
The proposed settlement will be evaluated by the union's board Friday and Saturday, then put before the 9,300 union members.
The industry expects union members to approve the settlement, but by a narrow margin.
Some factions within the pilots union have threatened to reject a proposal that offers any concessions on the regional jet issue.

While the pilots may be placated by a proposed wage offer, the regional jet issue have more far reaching implications, analysts said. The issue will likely resurface in four years when the proposed pact expires.
UAL Corp's United Airlines quickly resolved a dispute with is pilots by reaching a tentative labor pact that offered a 10 percent wage increase by July 1998.

American's pilots, however, are among the highest paid in the industry. The average American pilots makes $120,000, while United's pilots earn about $110,000 and Southwest Airlines Co's earn about $85,000.
"The case American made to the PEB was very compelling," Becker said.
The specifics of the settlement ultimately take a back seat to the greater issue at hand -- an end to bitter talks that have distracted American's management for months.

"There's a limited extent to which the specifics matter. What matters is that they just needed to reach an amicable agreement," said Edward Starkman, an analyst with Dillon Read. "If there was another strike, it would have caused deep problems that take years to recover from."
